text: Everything in this chapter so far has been about the mechanics of real hardware: picking a backend, transpiling for it, managing jobs, reading noisy results. This lesson is about the practical, career-relevant constraint that sits underneath all of it — you almost certainly have a limited amount of real hardware access, and how you spend it is a real engineering decision.

IBM Quantum Platform's free or open access tier comes with real limits on how much you can run — typically some form of monthly compute time or job allowance. The exact current limits change over time, so rather than repeating a number here that could be stale, the honest guidance is: check the IBM Quantum Platform's current plans page before you plan real hardware work, and treat whatever quota you're given as a real, finite budget, because it is one.

Queueing isn't uniform across all users. Paid tiers, Premium or pay-as-you-go plans, typically get priority over open, free-tier access on shared backends — two users submitting to the same backend at the same moment can see meaningfully different wait times purely based on account tier. That's worth knowing not to make you feel shortchanged, but because it's a realistic constraint to plan around.

Given limited quota and variable queue times, the right workflow is almost always: build and debug your circuit entirely on AerSimulator, since it's free and effectively instant, and you can run it as many times as you want while you iron out bugs. Only once you're confident the circuit is correct in simulation, submit it to real hardware — and batch as many validated circuits together into as few job submissions as possible. Submitting before you've validated in simulation is a common way to waste scarce quota on a bug you could have caught for free.

Think through your own limited quota concretely: which circuits have you validated thoroughly enough that a real-hardware run would tell you something genuinely new, rather than just catching a bug you could catch for free? Could any of your planned runs be combined into a single batched job? And is there a run you're tempted to make mainly out of curiosity, where simulation would actually answer your question just as well?

Chapter 6 moves on to the algorithms library built on everything this chapter covered — real, runnable implementations of Grover's algorithm, the quantum Fourier transform, and the variational algorithms that make use of parameterized circuits from Chapter 2.
